section.heading: The map
section.intro: Each band is money paid by one group to another in {year}. Its width is its size as a share of GDP, so wider means more. Select a group or a band to see what it is, how big it is and where the numbers come from.
section.introTs: Each band is one of the largest flows we have a yearly series for. Its width is its share of that year's GDP, on the same scale as the complete map.

framing: Gross flows can exceed GDP. GDP counts only final output once; the map also shows the inputs firms buy from each other and the money that passes through financial markets.

disc.D1: Household residual: the gap the national accounts publish between households' income and what they spend and save. The total is derived from published national-accounts figures; how it is split across household groups is estimated.
disc.D2: A reconciliation item between the national accounts and the balance of payments (the CIF adjustment on imports of services). It is not money paid abroad.
disc.D3_valuables: Derived: purchases of valuables, such as gold, that the national accounts do not assign to any sector.
disc.D3_si_errors: The rest of the saving-investment errors and omissions, after the valuables part: spread over companies and financial firms in proportion to their investment (estimated). The whole residual is derived from published national-accounts figures.
disc.D4: The GDP expenditure discrepancy. It is zero in {year}.

q.gst-states: Of every ₹100 of GST collected, how much do the States keep to spend?
q.gst-households: Of every ₹100 of GST, how much do households pay on what they buy for themselves?
q.bonds-banks: Of every ₹100 of new government bonds, how much did banks buy?
q.bonds-households: Of every ₹100 of new government bonds, how much did households buy directly?

why.gst-states: GST lands with the Centre and the States, and the Centre then passes part of its share on.
why.gst-households: Firms claim back most of the GST on their inputs, so the tax ends with final buyers.
why.bonds-banks: Banks hold government bonds as safe assets against their deposits.
why.bonds-households: Households lend to the government mostly indirectly: through deposits, insurance, pensions and small savings.
why.remit-gdp: Millions of small transfers add up to one of the largest flows into Indian households.
why.interest-gdp: Interest on past borrowing is one of the government's largest bills.
